lessons.title: Two numbers that refuse to be one
explanation: Latency is the time from starting one piece of work to finishing it. Throughput is how many pieces finish per unit time. They share a unit of time and they are not interchangeable. A bakery can take forty minutes to bake one loaf and still sell two hundred loaves an hour if two hundred loaves share the oven.

Hardware announcements collapse the two into a single 'speed'. Clock frequency is how fast one stage ticks — a latency story about a slice of one instruction. Instructions per cycle is how often useful work retires — a throughput story about the whole machine. You can raise the clock and lose throughput if every other cycle is a stall. You can lower the clock and gain throughput if you keep more independent work in flight.

The rest of this course is techniques for buying one quantity without pretending you bought the other. A pipeline overlaps stages so more instructions finish per second; each instruction still takes several stages. A cache attacks a long memory latency that would otherwise serialize the line. When someone says a chip got faster, ask which number moved.
lessons.example: A load from DRAM might take three hundred cycles. That is latency. A core that only issues that load retires almost nothing while it waits. If the machine has other independent work ready, those cycles can still retire useful results. The load is still slow. The machine is not idle. Throughput was protected; latency was not deleted.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every confused claim about clocks, cores, or 'more performance' is a latency/throughput mix-up. If you cannot say which quantity moved, you cannot read the claim, and you cannot choose the next technique.

quiz.stem: A change that only shrinks how long one instruction takes, leaving completions per cycle alone, primarily moved:

distractors.rationale: Throughput is completion rate, not per-item time.
How many instructions exist is not how long one takes.
Byte order is a naming convention, not a speed.

quiz.correctExplanation: Latency is per-item time. Throughput is how many items finish per unit time.
objectiveIds: Distinguish latency from throughput with a concrete pipeline or factory example

quiz.stem: An oven that needs 40 minutes per loaf and holds 200 loaves at once is mainly showing:

distractors.rationale: Each loaf still takes 40 minutes.

distractors.text: That clock frequency is the only knob
distractors.rationale: Overlap, not frequency, is doing the work here.

distractors.text: That the bakery has no capacity limit
distractors.rationale: The oven size is exactly the capacity that creates throughput.

quiz.correctExplanation: Each loaf still takes forty minutes. Many finish each hour because they overlap.
objectiveIds: Distinguish latency from throughput with a concrete pipeline or factory example

quiz.stem: Raising clock frequency can fail to raise completions per second when:
quiz.correctAnswer: The extra ticks are spent stalled, so useful work per cycle falls

distractors.text: Frequency and throughput are the same number
distractors.rationale: They are related and they are not the same number.

distractors.text: The instruction set has too few opcodes
distractors.rationale: ISA width is not what turns extra ticks into stalls.
An empty oven is a capacity story, not a stall-per-tick story.

quiz.correctExplanation: A faster tick on idle stages is a faster wait. Throughput needs useful retirements, not just a hotter clock.
objectiveIds: Explain why raising clock or width can move one without the other

lessons.title: A map is not a chain
explanation: Some programs are a chain: each step needs the previous result. Some programs are a map: the same operation on many independent elements. Colour every pixel, add two arrays, apply one force law to many particles. Independence is the property hardware can spend. If element 7 does not wait on element 3, you can run them together, or stagger them so a miss on 3 does not stall 7.

A loop-carried dependence (`x = f(x)`) is the opposite. No amount of extra arithmetic units deletes that edge. People say 'embarrassingly parallel' when the independence is obvious. Most real programs are mixed: a data-parallel map around a sequential reduction, or a grid of work that must meet at a barrier.

The skill is seeing which parts are maps. Hardware that bets on many simple pipelines only wins on the independent parts. A rewrite that turns a chain into a tree of partials is an algorithm change. The machine only runs the independence you actually created.
lessons.example: `out[i] = 2 * in[i]` is data-parallel: each index owns its element. `out[i] = out[i-1] + in[i]` is a chain. You can recover parallelism with a tree of partial sums, but that is a different algorithm. The original loop has a carried dependence the hardware cannot wish away.
lessons.whyItMatters: Wide machines are not faster sequential cores. They are machines for independent elements. If you cannot point at the independent work, you are about to be disappointed by a parallel launch.

quiz.correctAnswer: The same operation applies to independent elements

distractors.text: It is written as a for-loop
distractors.rationale: Loops can be sequential chains.

distractors.text: It uses a lot of memory
distractors.rationale: Traffic is not independence.
Frequency is a latency story, not a map.

quiz.correctExplanation: The hardware property is independence of elements, not the syntax of a loop.
objectiveIds: Recognize when a computation is data-parallel

quiz.stem: `x = f(x)` on every iteration is hard to widen because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Each step depends on the previous result

distractors.rationale: The cost is the dependence, not call overhead.
ISAs happily express sequential updates.
A chain is a dependence, not a missing oscillator.

quiz.correctExplanation: A loop-carried dependence is a chain. Extra units have nothing independent to do.
objectiveIds: Contrast that with a sequential dependence a GPU cannot wish away

quiz.stem: Rewriting a reduction as a tree of partials is an example of:
quiz.correctAnswer: Creating independence the original loop did not have

distractors.rationale: The rewrite is about dependence, not making memory slower.
Endianness does not manufacture parallelism.

distractors.text: Deleting the need for a clock
distractors.rationale: The algorithm still runs on a timed machine.

quiz.correctExplanation: The algorithm manufactures parallelism. Hardware cannot invent a missing independent edge.
objectiveIds: Contrast that with a sequential dependence a GPU cannot wish away

lessons.title: The part you cannot widen owns the speedup
explanation: Amdahl's argument is a conservation law, not a slogan. If a fraction s of the original time is serial — it cannot be widened — then even infinite parallel resources leave you with at least s of the original time. Speedup is at most 1/s. The parallel fraction can be made cheap. The leftover cannot.

People apply this backwards. They measure the part they accelerated, quote that number, and ignore the serial glue: setup, reduction, I/O, a lock, a single-threaded parser. The more you speed the wide part, the more the leftover dominates wall time. That is why a 100× kernel can produce a 2× program.

The useful move is to name s. Sometimes s is real physics (a loop-carried dependence). Sometimes s is an accident of the current algorithm (a sequential reduction you could rewrite as a tree). Amdahl does not tell you s is sacred. It tells you that whatever you leave serial will own the endgame.
lessons.example: A program spends 90% of its time in a map you can widen and 10% in a serial pass. Infinite workers make the map free. The program still takes 10% of the original time: speedup 10×, not infinity. If you only report the map, you will promise 100× and ship 10×.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every 'we parallelized it' claim needs the serial leftover in the same sentence. Otherwise you are quoting the part that got cheaper and hiding the part that now dominates.

quiz.stem: If a fraction s of the original time cannot be parallelized, Amdahl's bound on speedup is:

distractors.rationale: s is the leftover time, not the speedup.
Worker count does not lift the serial floor.
Amdahl is about the serial fraction, not the tick.

quiz.correctExplanation: Infinite workers make the parallel part free. You still pay s. Speedup ≤ 1/s.
objectiveIds: State Amdahl's bound as the serial fraction that remains

quiz.stem: A map that was 90% of runtime is made instant. The program's speedup is about:
quiz.correctAnswer: 10×, because the leftover 10% is now the whole run

distractors.text: 90×, because that is how much you accelerated
distractors.rationale: You deleted 90% of the original time, leaving 10%.

distractors.text: Infinite, because the map is gone
distractors.rationale: The serial pass is still there.
Vanishing work makes the program faster, not slower.

quiz.correctExplanation: Original 1.0 becomes 0.10. 1 / 0.10 = 10. The leftover owns the new runtime.
objectiveIds: Predict why speeding only the parallel part stops helping

quiz.stem: Further widening an already-tiny parallel remainder usually:
quiz.correctAnswer: Moves wall time very little, because the serial leftover dominates

distractors.rationale: Diminishing returns are the point of the bound.

distractors.text: Deletes the need for an algorithm
distractors.rationale: If s is an accident, rewrite s; more workers will not.
Amdahl is not a frequency knob.

quiz.correctExplanation: Once the map is cheap, extra workers polish a rounding error. Attack s, or stop.
objectiveIds: Predict why speeding only the parallel part stops helping

lessons.title: Time is instructions, CPI, and a tick
explanation: CPU time for a program factors as instruction count × cycles per instruction × clock period. That is bookkeeping, not a slogan. Instruction count is the compiler and the ISA. CPI is how many ticks the machine actually spends per retired instruction — stalls included. Clock period is how long a tick lasts.

IPC is 1/CPI when you mean useful retirements per cycle. Marketing quotes peak IPC. Reality is average CPI on this binary, with these misses and these branches. A machine can have a faster clock and a worse CPI and lose. Another can have a slower clock and retire more useful work per tick and win.

The three factors move separately. A compiler that emits fewer instructions can still lose if those instructions miss in cache and inflate CPI. A wider issue path can drop CPI only if there is independent work to issue. A frequency bump can raise power and leave CPI stuck on memory. When a review says 'faster', ask which factor moved.
lessons.example: Program A: 1.0e9 instructions, CPI 1.0, 2 GHz → 0.50 s. Program B: the same instructions, CPI 1.6 because of misses, 2.5 GHz → 0.64 s. The higher clock lost. The CPI story was the real one.
lessons.whyItMatters: Clock-only comparisons are how people misread every chip launch. Time has three factors. If you cannot name which one moved, you are reading a brochure.

distractors.rationale: Frequency is one factor, not the product.
Those may move CPI, they are not the identity.
How many operations exist is not how many this program retired.

quiz.correctExplanation: Count, cycles per instruction, and the length of a cycle. That is the identity.
objectiveIds: Factor time into instruction count, CPI, and clock period

quiz.stem: A chip with a higher clock can still take longer when:
quiz.correctAnswer: CPI rises enough that extra ticks do not buy extra useful work

distractors.rationale: A zero-instruction program is not the usual case.
Register count is not the failing factor here.

distractors.text: Throughput and latency are the same number
distractors.rationale: They are not, and that is a different lesson.

quiz.correctExplanation: Time is the product. A hotter clock times a fatter CPI can be a slower run.
objectiveIds: Explain why a higher clock can still lose performance

quiz.stem: Peak IPC in a slide deck is a poor predictor of this program because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Average CPI includes the stalls this binary actually hits

distractors.text: IPC is not related to CPI
distractors.rationale: IPC is the reciprocal of CPI when both mean useful work.
They can, and that is a different factor.

distractors.text: Clock period is always one nanosecond
distractors.rationale: Period varies; that is not why peak IPC lies.

quiz.correctExplanation: Peak assumes a fed machine. This binary's misses and branches are in the average.
objectiveIds: Explain why a higher clock can still lose performance
